title: School zone speed limits and speed cameras
subtitle: Also: 417 King West tower, rental replacement by-law, fireworks enforcement, park alcohol pilot, heritage designations, fire staffing.
overview: Council's longest debate was on school zone speed limits. School zones without automated speed enforcement (ASE) cameras stay at 30 km/h. Zones that have cameras, or get them later, will be set to 40 km/h. Council also asked staff to tell the Region of Waterloo that ASE should not operate on holidays. Councillors were frustrated that the Region, which runs the camera program, controls how the cameras operate.

Council adopted the planning approvals for a 55-storey development at 417 King Street West, with a maximum height of 535 metres above sea level to address Region and aviation concerns. Decisions on 20 Woolner Trail and on 93-99 Benton Street were deferred to January 22, 2024. Council directed staff to engage on a rental replacement by-law and approved a grant of up to $96,000 a year to The Working Centre for winter sidewalk clearing.

Council also increased minimum fire suppression staffing from 35 to 37 firefighters. It asked staff to expand fireworks education and enforcement, and to develop a pilot for alcohol in Victoria Park or another park. Fourteen properties will move toward heritage designation. After closed sessions, council directed staff to acquire a property for affordable housing and to proceed with a recreational facility project.

decisions.detail: Council kept 30 km/h in school zones without ASE and set 40 km/h in zones with ASE, now or when installed, as amended and carried {{vote:m3}}.
Council directed staff to tell the Region that ASE on Kitchener neighbourhood roads should not take place on holidays {{vote:m4}}.
Council adopted the official plan and zoning changes for a 55-storey mixed-use building, adding a maximum height of 535 metres above sea level.
Staff will engage the development industry and community stakeholders on a rental replacement by-law (Option 3) and keep working with the Region on displacement.
Subject to budget approval, council will give The Working Centre up to $96,000 a year for the winter sidewalk clearing program.
Council raised the minimum fire suppression staffing level from 35 to 37 firefighters, with a review when Fire Station 8 opens.
Staff will run a public education campaign and raise by-law officers on duty from 2 to 8 on days fireworks are permitted.
Staff will develop criteria for a pilot allowing open alcohol consumption in Victoria Park or another park, reporting by the end of Q2 2024.

debate: Supporters of the staff approach and a school travel planning delegate argued that school grounds are used well beyond school hours, and that consistent, lower speeds improve compliance and encourage walking and cycling.

Several councillors said they were uncomfortable with tickets for minor speeding in the evenings or on holidays, calling it punitive. They preferred 40 km/h on camera-enforced zones. Others said this put driver comfort ahead of child safety and weakened Vision Zero.

Staff said the Region operates the ASE program and the City cannot set its parameters, but it could run its own program. That would need a processing centre, a provincial offences court arrangement and a camera provider. Councillors voiced frustration at the Region's communication and at not sharing in ticket revenue.
On Woolner Trail, a delegate opposed to the application raised traffic counts and pedestrian safety on Fairway Road. The delegate supported deferral so staff could talk with the Region.
On the park alcohol pilot, councillors asked that the pilot dates stay flexible until staff finish their research. Staff said police, legal and risk questions need answers first.
